subject: mechanical
audience: FE Mechanical candidates and mechanical engineering students
title: The Fast-Looking Oil Flow That Was Still Laminar
featured_title: THE FAST-LOOKING OIL FLOW THAT WAS STILL LAMINAR

presentation.challenge: The oil was moving at 2 m/s, but its Reynolds number was only 1700.

practice.primary_question: Why can a fluid moving at 2 m/s still be in laminar pipe flow?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Classifying pipe flow from velocity alone without accounting for density, viscosity, and diameter.

case_dna.target_misconception: A pipe flow moving at 2 m/s must be turbulent because the velocity looks high.
case_dna.why_plausible: Velocity strongly affects Reynolds number, so it is easy to treat speed as the only indicator of turbulence.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For oil with density 850 kg/m³, dynamic viscosity 0.05 Pa·s, velocity 2 m/s, and diameter 0.05 m, Re=ρVD/μ=1700, which is in the laminar range.
case_dna.corrected_model: Pipe-flow regime depends on the dimensionless Reynolds number, not velocity alone.

problem_statement: Oil flows through a 50 mm diameter pipe at 2.0 m/s. The oil density is 850 kg/m³ and dynamic viscosity is 0.05 Pa·s. A technician labels the flow turbulent because 2 m/s seems fast. Calculate the Reynolds number, classify the flow, and determine what velocity would correspond to Re=4000 with the same oil and pipe.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The fluid moved quickly. Viscosity still kept the flow laminar.
gates.prompt: Which dimensionless quantity determines the pipe-flow regime?

options.label: Use Re=ρVD/μ and classify the flow from Re
options.reason: Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous effects.

options.label: Use velocity alone; 2 m/s is automatically turbulent
options.reason: The same velocity can produce different flow regimes for different fluids and diameters.

options.label: Use density alone to determine turbulence
options.reason: Reynolds number includes density, velocity, length scale, and viscosity.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the Reynolds number
gates.prompt: What Reynolds number results from the stated oil properties and pipe conditions?

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the Reynolds number
gates.success: Re=1700, which is laminar for ordinary internal-pipe-flow classification.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The dimensionless ratio explains the regime

cards.text: Re=85/0.05=1700, so viscosity is still influential enough for laminar behavior.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the flow-regime note
report: C1. The oil velocity is 2 m/s.
C2. The pipe diameter is 50 mm.
C3. Therefore the flow is turbulent because the velocity is high.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Flow regime cannot be classified from velocity alone.

evidence_choices.label: Re=ρVD/μ=1700
evidence_choices.reason: This is the governing dimensionless flow-regime parameter.

correction.template: The Reynolds number is about {re}, so the stated pipe flow is laminar.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Reach Re=4000 with the same oil and pipe
gates.constraint: Keep ρ, μ, and D unchanged.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply Reynolds-number scaling
gates.prompt: If velocity doubles while fluid properties and pipe diameter stay fixed, what happens to Reynolds number?

options.label: It doubles
options.reason: Re is directly proportional to V.

gates.explanation: With ρ, D, and μ fixed, Reynolds number scales linearly with velocity.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the flow-regime classification
gates.confirmation: I confirm that pipe-flow regime must be classified from Reynolds number rather than velocity alone.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The flow was labeled turbulent from speed alone.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Viscosity, density, and pipe diameter all affect the regime.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use Re=ρVD/μ before classifying internal flow.

seo.seo_title: Reynolds Number Pipe Flow: Why 2 m/s Can Still Be Laminar | FE E-054
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Mechanical Case E-054: oil flowing at 2 m/s in a 50 mm pipe has Reynolds number 1700 and remains laminar.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Mechanical Reynolds number pipe flow
seo.excerpt: A velocity that looks high does not guarantee turbulence. Viscosity and pipe size can keep Reynolds number low.
seo.direct_answer: For ρ=850 kg/m³, V=2 m/s, D=0.05 m, and μ=0.05 Pa·s, Re=ρVD/μ=1700. The flow is therefore laminar under the usual internal-pipe-flow classification.

faqs.q: Can 2 m/s pipe flow be laminar?
faqs.a: Yes. Flow regime depends on Reynolds number, not velocity alone.

faqs.q: What velocity gives Re=4000 for this oil and pipe?
